Tap a dot on Abbie, or tap her clothes
AW-STUDY-0059 · Wardrobe and backpack · for Evan's review

Dress Abbie by tapping her

A small bead sits on each part of Abbie you can change: her head, her top, her bottoms, her shoes, a little extra, and the backpack on her back. Tap a bead, or the part itself, and a short row of choices opens beside her. Tap one and she's wearing it. No menus and no walls of cards.

1. How do the choices open?

2. Which look?

This is a study: nothing here is in the game yet. Drag to turn her. Escape or a tap on the grass puts the choices away.

Recommendation

One grammar for everything she can wear or carry

  • Beads on the thing itself, choices beside it. This is the FPS gunsmith idea, the one the backpack and the buggy garage already use (simulations/loadout.mjs). You point at the part you want to change and see it change on her, live.
  • The wardrobe is separate from the backpack. Clothes are what she wears (only looks). The backpack is what she carries (her things, plus the plain upgrades from issue 535 that change what it can hold). The backpack shows up here as one bead on her back. Tapping it can swap its style, but its contents and upgrades stay in the backpack's own view (issue 536).
  • One grammar, a dialect per place. Liquid glass in the app and the HUD, wood and leaf in Winchester and the woods, and paper tags inside her notebook. The beads, the strip and the taps stay the same everywhere. Only the materials change, the way CLAUDE.md's place dialects ask.
  • Choices open beside her, not in a ring. The ring is fun, but it covers the very part you are dressing, and it breaks up with ten choices. Keep the ring for short lists of four or fewer, like hats.

Decision for Evan: pick the look (or a dialect per place), and confirm that clothes get their own wardrobe, apart from the backpack.

A · Recommended

Beads, and a strip beside her

The part stays in view while you choose, so every tap shows on her at once. It already works for the backpack and the buggy, and it reads well on a phone, where the strip drops below her.

B · Short lists only

A ring round the bead

It feels like a toy, and your thumb travels the least. But the ring sits on top of the very part you're changing, and with eight or more choices it grows bigger than she is. Try it above with the top or the shoes.

C · Not for us

A paper-doll list down the side

This is the classic RPG character sheet, with slots in a column next to the figure. It's precise, but it's a side panel: it covers a third of the world, it needs reading, and it's the facet menu Evan called unusable in issue 535.

Architecture

What she wears, what she carries, what it can do

WardrobeBackpack lookBackpack upgradesBackpack contents
What it isClothes: head, top, bottoms, shoes, an extraStyle, colour, pattern, pocket, straps, lining, notebookPlain upgrades: more pockets, a keyring (issue 535)Quest items, pickups, charms
KindCosmeticCosmeticFunctionalInventory
Changed byBeads on Abbie (this study)The bead on her back, or the backpack's own viewEarned by playing, picked in the backpack viewPlaying: picking up, using, quests
Stored inaw-wardrobe (new)aw-backpack (look)aw-backpack (upgrades)aw-inventory
Who reads itEverywhere she is drawn: FPS, minigames, introbackpack-wear.mjs, the left barThe inventory (capacity)Quests, directors, the voice controller (through the manifest)

Rules: a look never changes what she can carry, and an upgrade never changes how she looks, beyond the extra pocket you can see. Clothes are never items in the backpack. Tapping the bead on her back takes you to the backpack itself. Characters perceive what she is wearing (it's in the world), but the beads are on the presentation layer, so no bot ever sees a bead.

Touch and children

Made for small fingers that can't read yet

  • Every target is at least 44 points. A bead is drawn at 26 px, but it has a 44 px hit ring. On a touch screen the choices in the strip grow to 42 px with 8 px gaps (this study added that to the shared loadout.mjs).
  • You don't need words. Each choice is the thing itself (a colour, a hat, a shoe), and it shows on her the moment you tap it. Names appear only as a tooltip for grown-ups and in the VoiceOver labels.
  • Colour isn't the only clue. Clothes choices carry a small shape icon on top of their colour, so a child who can't tell red from green still sees which is which.
  • It's easy to get out. Tap the bead again, tap the grass, or press Escape. Nothing is lost, because every tap saves as you go.
  • Calm motion. With reduced motion on, the beads stop breathing and the strip simply appears.
  • One hand. On a phone the strip opens below her, within thumb reach, and never covers the part being dressed.
What it needs

Assets and data

  • Abbie's clothes as named parts on her figure, built as engineered low-poly geometry from a recipe, the way the Character Studio cast is (studies/character-studio/characters.mjs). Each part has a slot name (head, top, bottom, feet, extra) and its own material name. The figure in this study is a placeholder toy, not her final model.
  • Six to ten choices per slot to start: MJ proofs, then recipes, with each choice keeping its intent in its asset folder, per the modeler rules.
  • A shape icon for each choice, a small white silhouette drawn from the model so they always match.
  • A new store, aw-wardrobe: {head, top, bottom, feet, extra} with option ids, plus a default (Evan's pick, the way the backpack has DEFAULT_LOOK).
  • One function to wear the outfit, wearOutfit(figure), next to wearBackpack(), so every game that shows her dresses her the same way.
  • Unlocks, later: some clothes could be charm rewards (a space helmet for the Moon Mission). Clothes still never count as backpack items.
Next steps

After Evan picks

  1. Evan picks the look (or a dialect per place) and confirms the wardrobe is its own thing, apart from the backpack.
  2. Make proofs for her first clothes in Midjourney, one sheet per slot, and get his picks.
  3. Build her figure's clothes as recipe parts, with aw-wardrobe and wearOutfit().
  4. Put the wardrobe in the game: a small figure of her on the left bar next to the backpack (the things she can touch). Tapping it brings her into focus with her beads, the same way the backpack comes out.
  5. Wire the bead on her back to the backpack view (issue 536), so it's one tap from her clothes to her things.
Design card
What the player feels: "I made Abbie look like me today."
How would the character know? She's wearing it. Townsfolk can notice a new hat, and the clothes are in the world.
Mode: spatial (the beads sit on the person they're about), with the strip as the one bit of overlay, because choosing needs precision. "None" can't dress her, and diegetic (a mirror in her bedroom) is a lovely later way in, but it's slow for every change.
Who it's for: the player (the child).
The whole game adapts: she wears the outfit in every game. A rain coat or a space helmet can match the weather or the Moon.
Way of acting: HUD and app, summoned from the left bar. It's not a card and not a tile.
